title: Hard Cider Hangover: Why Cider Hits Hard and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Why do cider hangovers feel so bad? How strength, sweetness, fizz, methanol, and fruit sugars add up, why cider can give you a headache, and how to drink it smarter.
metaDescription: Why cider hangovers feel so bad: strength, sweetness, fizz, methanol and fruit sugars. Plus why cider gives you a headache and how to avoid it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** hard cider doesn't contain some special hangover toxin, but it stacks several things against you at once. It's often stronger than people assume (many ciders run 5 to 7 percent alcohol, and some go well past that), it's usually sweet enough to hide the taste of the alcohol, it's fizzy, and it's poured in pints. Apples also bring their own baggage: more methanol than grain-based drinks, plenty of fruit sugars that some guts handle badly, and in most commercial ciders, added sulfites. Put together, it's very easy to drink more alcohol than you meant to, faster than you meant to, with a sugar load on top. That's the real reason cider hangovers have a reputation.

**The quick rules:** Treat a pint of cider like a pint of strong beer, not a soft drink. Check the alcohol percentage on the can or tap list, because it varies a lot. Pick dry styles over sweet ones when you can. Eat before you drink, alternate each cider with a glass of water, and stop earlier than you would with a lighter beer. If cider gives you a headache after just one glass, that's a sign of a sensitivity worth paying attention to, not a hangover.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most cider hangovers are miserable but harmless, and they pass within a day. Get medical help if you have vomiting you can't stop or can't keep water down for several hours, confusion, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, seizures, trouble breathing, or you can't stay awake. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning, and you should call 911 (in the US) or your local emergency number. See a doctor soon (not urgently) if you get hives, facial swelling, wheezing, or a pounding headache after small amounts of cider, because that points to a reaction to something in the drink rather than too much alcohol. And if you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick in the hours after you stop drinking and those feelings go away when you drink again, tell a doctor plainly. That pattern can be early alcohol withdrawal, which deserves proper medical care, not a hangover remedy.

## Why Cider Hangovers Feel So Bad

A hangover comes mainly from how much alcohol you drank and how fast. Dehydration, poor sleep, an irritated stomach, low blood sugar, and your immune system's reaction to alcohol all play a part. On top of that, by-products in the drink itself (called congeners) can make it worse. Cider doesn't change those basics. What it does is make several of them more likely at the same time.

Here are the main reasons cider has its reputation, roughly in order of how much they likely matter.

### 1. It's stronger than it tastes

This is the big one. Most mainstream hard ciders sit somewhere around 4.5 to 7 percent alcohol by volume (ABV). Craft, farmhouse, and "imperial" ciders can run 8 percent or higher, and ice cider and apple wine go higher still. Compare that with a typical light lager at around 4 to 5 percent.

The trouble is that cider rarely tastes as strong as it is. The fruit and sugar cover the alcohol, so it drinks like juice. A 16-ounce pint of 6.5 percent cider holds noticeably more alcohol than a 12-ounce bottle of regular beer, often closer to one and a half or two standard drinks. If you count "one cider" as "one drink," you're probably undercounting.

A quick way to check: multiply the ounces in your glass by the ABV, then divide by 0.6 (the ounces of pure alcohol in one US standard drink).

| Drink | Size | ABV | Roughly how many standard drinks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light lager | 12 oz | 4.2% | about 0.8 |
| Regular beer | 12 oz | 5% | about 1 |
| Typical hard cider | 12 oz can | 5.5% | about 1.1 |
| Pub pint of cider | 16 oz | 6.5% | about 1.7 |
| Strong craft cider | 16 oz | 8% | about 2.1 |
| UK pint of cider | 20 oz (568 ml) | 5% | about 1.7 |

Three or four pints of a 6 to 7 percent cider adds up to six or seven standard drinks without much effort. That alone is enough to explain a rough morning.

### 2. Sweetness hides the alcohol and encourages faster drinking

Sweet drinks go down easily. You tend to drink them faster, sip them more like a soft drink, and notice the effects later. Many mainstream ciders are back-sweetened after fermentation, and sweet styles commonly carry somewhere in the high teens to mid-20s of grams of sugar per 12-ounce serving. Check the label of your brand, because it ranges widely from bone-dry to dessert-sweet.

Faster drinking means your blood alcohol rises more quickly and peaks higher. A higher peak is closely tied to worse hangovers. So the sugar matters less as a "sugar hangover" and more because it makes the alcohol so easy to drink.

### 3. Carbonation may speed things up

Most ciders are fizzy. There's some evidence that carbonated alcoholic drinks are absorbed into the blood faster than flat ones for some people. One frequently cited small study from 2007 found that most participants reached a higher blood alcohol level after a carbonated drink than after the same amount of alcohol without bubbles, though a few people showed no difference. The effect isn't large or consistent, but it nudges in the same direction as everything else: alcohol hitting you sooner. We cover this in more detail in [does carbonation make you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-carbonation-make-you-drunk-faster).

### 4. Apples make more methanol than grains

This is the part that's specific to fruit. Apples are rich in pectin, a natural fiber in fruit skins and flesh. During fermentation, enzymes break pectin down and release small amounts of **methanol**. That's why fruit-based drinks such as cider, fruit wines, and fruit brandies generally contain more methanol than beer or vodka.

The amounts in commercial cider are small and well within safety limits. This is not the dangerous methanol you hear about in bootleg spirits. But methanol is one of the congeners researchers have linked to hangover severity. The leading idea is that your body breaks methanol down into formaldehyde and formic acid, and that this happens mostly after the ethanol (the main alcohol) has cleared, which lines up with the timing of the worst hangover symptoms the next morning. This is a plausible theory with some supporting research, not a settled fact. For the bigger picture, see our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### 5. Sulfites, which matter for a small group of people

Most commercial ciders, like most wines, have sulfites added to stop unwanted yeast and bacteria and keep the flavor stable. Bottles in the US must carry a "contains sulfites" label when levels pass a small threshold.

For most people, sulfites aren't a real hangover factor. A minority of people, especially some with asthma, are genuinely sulfite-sensitive and can get wheezing, flushing, or hives. Whether sulfites cause headaches in people without that sensitivity is much less clear. Our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) explains why sulfites usually take more blame than they deserve. The same reasoning applies to cider.

### 6. Fruit sugars that some guts don't handle well

Apples are high in fructose and also contain sorbitol, a sugar alcohol that's well known for causing gas, bloating, and loose stools in larger amounts. Pears are even richer in sorbitol, so perry (pear cider) can be harder on some stomachs. People with fructose malabsorption or irritable bowel syndrome often notice that sweet ciders and apple juice set them off.

Alcohol already irritates the stomach and gut. Add a big dose of fruit sugars and you can end up with the bloated, crampy, "my stomach is the worst part of this" version of a hangover. If that sounds familiar, it may be the apples, not just the alcohol.

### 7. It's often a drink of long, sunny days

This isn't chemistry, but it's real. Cider is a classic drink for festivals, beer gardens, barbecues, and long afternoons outside. That usually means hours of steady drinking, heat, sweating, and not much water or food. Dehydration and a long session do far more to your morning than the apples do.

## Cider Headache: Why Cider Gives Some People a Headache

A lot of people searching for a cider hangover are really asking about a cider headache. There are two different kinds, and they have different causes.

**The next-morning headache** is the classic hangover headache. It's mostly driven by the amount of alcohol, dehydration, poor sleep, and the body's inflammatory response to alcohol. Because cider is easy to over-drink, it's an easy drink to get this headache from. For how this works and what helps, see our guide to the [alcohol headache](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025).

**The headache that starts during or soon after one glass** is different. If a single cider leaves you with a throbbing head within an hour or two, that's not a hangover. Possible culprits include:

- **Alcohol itself.** Alcohol widens blood vessels and is a well-known trigger for migraines and cluster headaches in people prone to them. For some, any alcohol at all can do this.
- **Biogenic amines such as histamine and tyramine.** These form during fermentation. Cider usually has less histamine than red wine, but levels vary by how it's made, and people with histamine intolerance can react to small amounts. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) covers the signs.
- **Sulfites**, in the small group of people who are truly sensitive.
- **Phenolic compounds and tannins** from cider apples, especially in traditional and farmhouse styles made from bittersweet apple varieties. Some people link their headaches to these, though the evidence is thin.

If you get headaches from small amounts of cider but not from the same amount of alcohol in a clear spirit, keep a simple note of what you drank, how much, and when the headache started. Over a few weeks that tells you more than any article can. If the headaches are severe, come with other symptoms, or are getting more frequent, mention them to a doctor.

## Is Cider Worse Than Beer for a Hangover?

Not automatically. Drink for drink, at the same alcohol content and the same pace, the difference between cider and beer is probably modest. Both are fermented drinks with their own congeners. Beer has its own sources of headache trouble, as we cover in our [beer hangover](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) guide.

The practical differences tend to favor beer in real life, though:

- Cider is often stronger per glass than the beer people would otherwise drink.
- Sweet cider is easier to drink quickly.
- Cider has more methanol from fruit pectin.
- Sweet cider carries a lot more sugar, which can upset the stomach and make you feel worse the next day.

So the honest answer is that cider is rarely worse *because it's cider*. It's worse because of how people end up drinking it. If you drink a dry, 5 percent cider slowly with food, you'll likely feel about the same as with a similar amount of beer.

## Is Cider Worse Than Wine or Spirits?

Compared with red wine, cider usually has fewer congeners like tannins and histamine, though more than a clean spirit. Compared with a clear spirit like vodka mixed with soda water, cider generally has more congeners and much more sugar. Research comparing high-congener and low-congener drinks (bourbon versus vodka, for example) has found somewhat worse hangovers with the darker, more congener-rich drinks at the same blood alcohol level, though the difference was smaller than many people expect. Cider falls somewhere in the middle of that range.

The bigger point stays the same. The amount and speed of drinking matter much more than the type of drink. Switching from cider to vodka won't save you if you drink twice as much.

## Sweet Cider vs Dry Cider: Does It Matter?

It can, for a few reasons.

**Dry ciders** have had most of their sugar fermented out. They taste more like a crisp white wine, they're harder to gulp, and they won't load your stomach with fructose and sorbitol. If you like cider and want to keep drinking it, dry styles are generally the gentler choice.

**Sweet and flavored ciders** (berry, rosé, ginger, and so on) are usually back-sweetened with juice, sugar, or syrups. They're easy to drink fast, and the sugar can add to nausea and stomach upset.

**Low-sugar or "zero sugar" ciders** typically use non-sugar sweeteners. They cut the sugar problem, but they're still alcohol. One study on diet versus regular mixers found that people reached higher breath alcohol with the diet mixer, likely because sugar slows how fast the stomach empties. That research was on mixed spirits, not cider, so don't read too much into it. The lesson is simply that "less sugar" doesn't mean "less hangover."

A simple check is the label. Many cider makers list sugar per serving or use a dryness scale. If not, the words "dry," "brut," or "extra dry" are a reasonable guide.

## Is Hard Cider Gluten-Free?

Hard cider made only from apples (or pears) is naturally gluten-free, which is one reason it's popular with people avoiding gluten. A few products add barley malt or are made in shared facilities, so if you have celiac disease, check the label or the maker's website. Note that gluten has nothing to do with hangovers for people who don't have celiac disease or a real gluten sensitivity. For more, see our [gluten-free alcohol](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) guide.

## How to Avoid a Cider Hangover

None of these is magic. Together, they make a big difference.

1. **Check the ABV and count honestly.** Look at the percentage on the can or tap list. Use the table above to translate pints into standard drinks. This one habit does more than everything else on this list.
2. **Choose smaller servings.** A half-pint or a 12-ounce can instead of a pint cuts each round by a third or more.
3. **Pick drier, lower-strength styles.** A dry 4.5 to 5 percent cider is a very different night from a sweet 7 percent one.
4. **Eat a proper meal first.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which lowers your peak.
5. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per cider. On a hot day outside, drink more.
6. **Slow your pace.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour. Your liver clears roughly that much, and trying to outpace it is what produces the worst mornings.
7. **Don't mix cider with shots.** Adding spirits to a cider session is where many people lose count.
8. **Stop a few hours before bed.** Alcohol close to bedtime wrecks the second half of your sleep, which makes every hangover feel worse.
9. **If cider sweetness upsets your stomach, switch styles.** Try a dry cider, or skip it on nights you know you'll be drinking for hours.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes deeper on the habits with the best evidence.

## What Helps the Morning After Cider

There's no cure for a hangover, so the goal is to support your body while it recovers.

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is fine. An electrolyte drink can help if you sweated a lot or have been sick. Sip rather than gulp if your stomach is unsettled.
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, crackers, eggs, bananas, or soup. Gentle food helps your blood sugar and your stomach.
- **Go easy on more sugar.** If sweet cider left your gut bloated and crampy, a sugary breakfast drink can make it worse. Plain foods are kinder.
- **Pain relief, carefully.** If you need something for a headache, a standard dose of ibuprofen with food is a common choice, but NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver after drinking, and you shouldn't take it while alcohol is still in your system. Our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide explains why. If you take other medicines or have stomach, kidney, or liver problems, ask a pharmacist.
- **Rest.** Sleep is where most of the recovery happens. If you can, take it slow.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another cider only delays the hangover and adds to the total.

## When a Cider Hangover Is Something More

Most of the time, a bad morning after cider is just a bad morning. But some symptoms are a sign that something else is going on.

**Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone:**

- Is vomiting repeatedly and can't keep fluids down
- Is confused, very drowsy, or can't be woken
- Has slow or irregular breathing, bluish or pale skin, or a seizure
- Has a very low body temperature

These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't let them "sleep it off." Stay with them, keep them on their side, and get help.

**See a doctor if:**

- Small amounts of cider cause hives, flushing, swelling, wheezing, or a severe headache. That suggests an allergy or sensitivity to something in the drink.
- Your stomach pain is severe, sits in your upper belly or under your right ribs, or keeps coming back after drinking.
- Your hangovers are getting worse or lasting longer than they used to, especially after drinks that never bothered you before.
- You get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or nauseated after you stop drinking, and a drink makes it better. Say this to a doctor directly. It can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which can become serious and is treatable.

## Where DHM Fits In

If cider is your drink of choice and you want extra help, some people use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. It has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. The honest picture: most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own, and it does nothing to make a 7 percent pint weaker. It is not a substitute for drinking less, eating, and hydrating.

If you want to try it as part of a sensible plan, two popular options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly single-ingredient pick, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Cider hangovers are mostly about **how much alcohol you drink and how fast**, and cider makes it unusually easy to drink a lot quickly.
- Many ciders are 5 to 7 percent ABV or more, and a pint can be close to two standard drinks.
- Apples add more methanol than grain drinks, plenty of fructose and sorbitol for sensitive guts, and usually sulfites. These matter less than the alcohol but can make the morning worse.
- A headache after one glass isn't a hangover. It points to a sensitivity worth tracking.
- Dry, lower-strength ciders, smaller servings, food, water, and a slower pace are your best defense.
- Know the emergency signs of alcohol poisoning, and take withdrawal-type symptoms to a doctor.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) and our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does cider give me such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because it's easy to drink a lot of alcohol quickly. Many hard ciders are 5 to 7 percent alcohol or more, the sweetness hides the taste of alcohol, it's carbonated, and it's served in pints, so one pint can be close to two standard drinks. Apples also produce more methanol than grains, and sweet ciders carry a lot of fruit sugar that can upset your stomach. Those extras likely play a smaller role than the total amount of alcohol.

**Why does cider give me a headache?**

A next-morning headache is usually a normal hangover from the amount of alcohol, dehydration, and poor sleep. A headache that starts during or shortly after one glass is different. It can come from alcohol itself acting as a migraine trigger, from histamine and other amines formed during fermentation, or, in a small group of people, from sulfites. If small amounts reliably cause headaches, keep notes on what you drank and mention it to a doctor.

**Is cider worse than beer for a hangover?**

Not automatically. At the same alcohol content and the same pace, the difference is probably small. In practice cider often causes worse hangovers because it tends to be stronger per glass, easier to drink fast, sweeter, and higher in methanol from fruit pectin. A dry 5 percent cider drunk slowly with food will likely feel about the same as a similar amount of beer.

**Is dry cider better than sweet cider for avoiding a hangover?**

Generally yes. Dry ciders have less sugar, are harder to gulp, and are easier on the stomach because they carry less fructose and sorbitol. Sweet and flavored ciders are easy to drink quickly and the extra sugar can add to nausea and bloating. Either way, the alcohol content and how much you drink matter most.

**How many standard drinks are in a pint of cider?**

It depends on the strength. A 16-ounce US pint of 6.5 percent cider is about 1.7 standard drinks, and an 8 percent cider in the same glass is about 2.1. A UK pint (568 ml) of 5 percent cider is about 1.7 US standard drinks. To check any drink, multiply the ounces by the alcohol percentage and divide by 0.6.

**Does cider contain methanol?**

Yes, in small amounts. Apples are rich in pectin, and during fermentation pectin breaks down and releases some methanol. That's why fruit-based drinks generally contain more methanol than beer or vodka. The levels in commercial cider are low and within safety limits, but methanol is one of the congeners researchers have linked to hangover severity.

**Is hard cider gluten-free?**

Cider made only from apples or pears is naturally gluten-free. Some products add barley malt or are made in shared facilities, so people with celiac disease should check the label or the maker's information. Gluten doesn't affect hangovers for people without celiac disease or a real gluten sensitivity.

**When should I see a doctor after drinking cider?**

Call 911 if someone has repeated vomiting, confusion, can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, or has a seizure, since those are signs of alcohol poisoning. See a doctor if small amounts cause hives, swelling, wheezing, or severe headaches, if you get severe upper belly pain, or if you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious after you stop drinking and a drink makes it better, which can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal.
